passage:
Your father's elder sister, Sachin, your Mohini Bua. You've heard she was "away" for three years. Let me tell you what that was.
I, Kamal, was twenty-six, her elder brother; she was twenty-four. She joined a group in Pune. At first it was only weekends. Then she stopped arguing about anything. Every sentence was "the Master says" or "the unawakened". She skipped Diwali.
I was furious. I told her on the phone, "Leave them or don't come home." She didn't come home. Not for two years.
It was your Dadi who kept writing to her. Every month, a short letter. Nothing about the group. The mango tree, your father's exams, the dog. "The door is open, beta."
When Mohini finally left, she came to Dadi's door, not mine.
I was right that the group was bad for her. I was wrong about everything else.

qa.q: What did Kamal tell Mohini on the phone?
qa.a: Kamal told Mohini, "Leave them or don't come home."

qa.q: How did young Kamal feel as Mohini changed?
qa.a: Kamal was furious and frightened for Mohini, and that anger came out as an ultimatum rather than warmth.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story kept a way back open for Mohini?
qa.a: Dadi's monthly letters about ordinary things, never about the group, ending with "The door is open, beta", gave Mohini somewhere to return.

qa.q: How might Mohini have heard Kamal's ultimatum?
qa.a: Mohini likely heard it as rejection, which made the group seem like her only family and kept her away for two years.

grounding: An elder recalls noticing his sister change inside a controlling group, how his ultimatum pushed her away, and how steady warmth kept a door open.

passage:
Aadhya's train back to Nagpur left at 6:15, which gave Lavanya forty minutes at the station café.
Her younger sister looked well. Neat clothes, calm face. But every answer came out in the same shape. "Our teacher says doubt is just fear." "That's an outsider question, didi." She hadn't called their mother since March.
Lavanya felt the words rising in her throat: You've been brainwashed. Choose, them or us. She had rehearsed them on the bus.
Instead she pushed the plate of samosas across. "Do you remember how you used to eat only the corners?"
Aadhya smiled, a real smile, for one second.
At the platform announcement, Lavanya hugged her. "Whatever happens, you can call me. Anytime. No questions first."
Aadhya held on a moment longer than Lavanya expected. Then she was gone.
On the bus home, Lavanya cried, and then called their mother.

qa.q: What time did Aadhya's train leave?
qa.a: Aadhya's train left at 6:15.

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling as the rehearsed words rose in her throat?
qa.a: Lavanya felt angry and afraid for her sister, wanting to demand a choice, even though she held it back.

qa.q: Why was offering the samosas a wise choice in the short time they had?
qa.a: It reached the sister Lavanya knew from before, drew a real smile, and kept the door open, where an ultimatum would likely have pushed Aadhya closer to the group.

qa.q: What does Aadhya's longer hug suggest about how she received Lavanya's warmth?
qa.a: It suggests some part of Aadhya still wants her sister and heard the promise to call anytime, even while she talks in the group's language.

grounding: A woman notices her younger sister now speaks only the group's language, resists an ultimatum under time pressure, and offers steady warmth instead.

passage:
At Sunday lunch in their Pune flat, Nandini watched her younger sister and barely recognised her. Alka no longer argued about films or politics. Every answer came in the same smooth phrases: "That's low energy." "The Guide says doubt is fear." She had left her book club, and her oldest friend had stopped calling.
Papa put down his spoon. "Enough. Either you leave that group or you don't come to this house."
Alka stood up, very calm. "They told me you'd say this." She picked up her bag and left.
That night Nandini didn't send an article or a warning. She sent a photo of the two of them as kids on a scooter and wrote: "Whatever you choose, you're my sister. Mangoes on Saturday?"
Three days passed before the reply came. "Maybe." Nandini felt her chest loosen, just a little.

qa.q: What did Papa tell Alka at lunch?
qa.a: 'Either you leave that group or you don't come to this house.'

qa.q: What was Nandini feeling when Alka's 'Maybe' finally came?
qa.a: Nandini felt a small, careful relief, her chest loosening after three days of waiting and worry.

qa.q: Why might Nandini's message work better than Papa's ultimatum?
qa.a: It offered steady warmth and an ordinary plan without arguing, keeping a door open, while the ultimatum matched what the group had predicted.

qa.q: How might Alka have heard Papa's ultimatum?
qa.a: Alka seemed to hear it as proof of what the group said, 'They told me you'd say this', which likely pulled her closer to them.

grounding: Shows a sister noticing a sibling stop questioning and speak in a group's phrases, and how an ultimatum drives her away while warmth keeps a door open.

"You missed Ravi's wedding, you skipped Nani's birthday, and you keep saying 'the outside world'," Chaitanya said. "What happened to you, Vaibhav?"
"Nothing happened. I woke up."
"Woke up? You used to argue with me about everything. Now you just quote Brother Sam."
"Brother Sam says arguing is ego."
"See? That. Your group is a—"
Vaibhav's face shut like a door. "I knew you'd attack them. They warned me."
Chaitanya stopped and took a breath. "Okay. I'm sorry. I don't want to fight. I miss you, that's all."
Silence.
"Remember our Thursday badminton?"
"...Yeah."
"Court's still booked. Six o'clock. No questions about anything. Just badminton."
Vaibhav picked at the sofa cover. "Maybe."
"Maybe is good," Chaitanya said, and passed him the plate of pakoras.

qa.q: What time is the badminton court booked?
qa.a: Six o'clock.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya feeling when Vaibhav's face shut like a door?
qa.a: Chaitanya felt alarmed and sorry, seeing that the attack had confirmed the group's warning, so Chaitanya stopped and apologised.

qa.q: Which choice kept a door open, and why?
qa.a: Apologising, saying 'I miss you', and offering badminton with no questions; it gives Vaibhav a safe link to the old life without a fight.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav have felt when Chaitanya started attacking the group?
qa.a: Vaibhav likely felt defensive and proven right, since 'They warned me', which pushed him further toward the group.

grounding: Shows a relative noticing someone quote a group's language and cut family ties, and learning that attack backfires while warmth keeps a door open.

passage:
I'm Vishal, Yash's bhaiya, and I got it wrong before I got it right.
Last year Yash, who used to take apart every argument at dinner, stopped questioning anything. He spoke in the group's words: "alignment", "the pure ones", "the sleeping world". He dropped his cricket friends, then his job.
My first move was anger. I printed articles about the group and threw them on his bed. I said, "Choose. Them or us." He chose them. He didn't call for two months.
Then I changed tactics, or really, I stopped having tactics. Every Sunday I sent a short message: a photo of Ma's garden, the cricket score, "Thinking of you." No questions, no links.
In March he replied: "Is Ma's jasmine flowering?" I cried in the parking lot at work. Then I typed back, "Come and see it."

qa.q: What did Vishal throw on Yash's bed?
qa.a: Printed articles about the group.

qa.q: How did Vishal feel when Yash asked about Ma's jasmine?
qa.a: Vishal felt overwhelmed with relief and cried in the parking lot, because the reply meant the door was still open.

qa.q: What worked better than the ultimatum, and why?
qa.a: Short, warm Sunday messages with no questions or links; they kept a gentle bond without giving Yash anything to push against.

qa.q: How might Yash have seen the 'Them or us' ultimatum?
qa.a: Yash likely saw it as an attack that proved the group right, so choosing them felt like the only answer.

grounding: Shows an older brother noticing his sibling adopt a group's language and cut ties, learning that anger deepened the bond while steady warmth reopened contact.

passage:
Family counselling note, Thursday.
Usha came in about her son Pankaj, who joined a meditation "family" eight months ago. She described the changes: he no longer argues or questions anything; he calls his old friends "lower-energy people" and has stopped seeing them; most sentences now include the group's words, such as "surrender" and "the Source". He moved into the group's house in March.
In April his father gave him an ultimatum: "Them or us." Pankaj left the dinner table and did not call for six weeks. Usha said, "We pushed him right into their arms."
We talked about staying steady instead: short, warm messages without arguments, his favourite food on Sundays, no insults about the group, and a clear line that home is always open. Usha agreed to try, and to bring her husband next time.
Yesterday Usha sent Pankaj a photo of the mango tree in the yard. He replied with a heart.

qa.q: What did Pankaj's father say in April?
qa.a: He said, “Them or us.”

qa.q: How does Usha feel about the ultimatum now?
qa.a: Usha feels regretful and sad, believing the family pushed Pankaj right into the group's arms.

qa.q: What plan did Usha agree to try?
qa.a: Short, warm messages without arguments, his favourite food on Sundays, no insults about the group, a clear message that home is open, and bringing her husband next time.

qa.q: How might Pankaj have experienced the ultimatum?
qa.a: Pankaj probably felt attacked and forced to choose, which made the group seem like the only place that accepted him, so he stayed away six weeks.

grounding: Shows relatives noticing someone stop questioning, cut ties and speak in a group's language, and learning that warmth keeps the door open where ultimatums did not.
